title: Optimal dimension dependence in the smoothed complexity of the simplex method
credit: Bach, Huiberts, Optimal smoothed analysis of the simplex method, arXiv:2504.04197 (2025; v2 May 2026).
premise_risks: arXiv:2504.04197 (Bach-Huiberts; v2 May 2026, refereed status not verified): source of both the upper bound σ^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n and the diameter lower bound.
plain: Bach and Huiberts (2025) found a simplex method with smoothed complexity O(σ^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n) pivots and showed σ^{-1/2} is optimal. In the dimension d, the best lower bound is only about d^{1/2}. Close the gap in d.
math: Model: rows (ā_i, b̄_i) ∈ ℝ^{d+1}, i ≤ n, of Euclidean norm ≤ 1, each perturbed by independent N(0, σ² I), giving P = {x : ⟨a_i,x⟩ ≤ b_i}. Let diam(P) be the combinatorial diameter of its vertex-edge graph. Known (Bach–Huiberts): E[diam] = Ω(σ^{-1/2} d^{1/2} (ln 4/σ)^{-1/4}) at n = ⌊(4/σ)^d⌋, and a simplex method with O(σ^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n) pivots exists. Claim: there are b > 1/2, c > 0 and K such that for all large d and all 0 < σ ≤ 1/d, some n ≤ (4/σ)^{Kd} and some unperturbed rows of norm ≤ 1 give E[diam(P)] ≥ c σ^{-1/2} d^b (log 4/σ)^{-K}. (The companion algorithmic question, whether a polynomial-time-per-pivot rule with Phase I achieves O(σ^{-1/2} d^a (log n)^{O(1)}) for some a < 11/4, has no canonical formal model and is not part of Claim.)

title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
plain: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
math: Let N = 2^n, K = 2^{n-1}+1, d = ⌈√n⌉ − 1. SENS_n is the CNF on main variables x_v (v ∈ {0,1}^n) and sequential-counter variables s_{i,j} (0 ≤ i ≤ N, 0 ≤ j ≤ K). It consists of (i) the counter clauses (s_{N,K}); (¬s_{0,j}) for 1 ≤ j ≤ K; (¬s_{i,j} ∨ s_{i−1,j} ∨ x_i) and (¬s_{i,j} ∨ s_{i−1,j} ∨ s_{i−1,j−1}) for 1 ≤ i ≤ N, 1 ≤ j ≤ K, with x_1,…,x_N the main variables in a fixed order; together these say ∑_v x_v ≥ K; and (ii) the clauses ¬x_v ∨ ⋁_{u∈U} ¬x_u for every v and every (d+1)-set U of neighbours of v. Its size is N^{O(1)}: Θ(N·K) counter clauses plus N^{1+o(1)} neighbourhood clauses. It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does SENS_n have refutations of size N^{O(1)} in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes (size counted in bits), or (c) sum-of-squares of degree O(log N)? Claim: at least one of (a), (b), (c) holds. Each part is also stated separately. Lower bounds 2^{N^{Ω(1)}} are equally of interest.

title: Three collinear points after the fall of 3SUM
credit: Alman & Vassilevska Williams, 'Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs', arXiv:2610.06783 (2026), Sec. 1 and Sec. 6.
premise_risks: AVW arXiv:2610.06783 (2026 preprint): truly subquadratic 3SUM, the premise that removes the 3SUM-based lower bound for collinearity.
Majdoddin arXiv:2610.17420 (2026 preprint): improved thin-matrix-product reductions for 3SUM/APSP; supporting background.
Chan–Itakura–Ma–Yu arXiv:2610.42012 (2026 preprint): derandomization of real 3SUM; supporting background.
Fischer arXiv:2610.32162 (2026 preprint): k-AP-based GeomBase lower bounds explicitly not covering collinearity; used to argue the question is still open.
plain: Given n points in the plane (integer coordinates poly(n), or real RAM), decide whether three are collinear in O(n^{2-eps}) time for some eps>0; or give a fine-grained reduction showing Collinearity is hard under a hypothesis not refuted by Alman-Vassilevska Williams (e.g. 4SUM, 3SUM-Indexing, or a new geometric hypothesis).
math: Prove or disprove: for every constant c ≥ 1 there are ε > 0 and a deterministic word-RAM algorithm (word size Θ(log n)) deciding in O(n^{2-ε}) time whether n distinct points of ℤ² ∩ [−n^c, n^c]² contain three collinear points. (The real-RAM variant is a separate question.)
refs: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs, arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct 2026)
Majdoddin, Thin matrix products up to D<=N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, arXiv:2610.17420 (Oct 2026)
Gajentaan, Overmars, On a class of O(n^2) problems in computational geometry, CGTA 1995

title: Chaos in the double pendulum at every energy
plain: The planar double pendulum with equal masses and equal arms looks chaotic at moderate energies but almost regular at very low and very high energies. Prove that it has genuine (positive-entropy) chaos at every energy above the rest state.
math: Let $H(\theta_1,\theta_2,p_1,p_2)$ be the Hamiltonian of the planar double pendulum with $m_1=m_2=\ell_1=\ell_2=g=1$ on $T^*\mathbb T^2$, with minimum value $E_0$ (the hanging rest state). Prove that for every $E>E_0$ the Hamiltonian flow restricted to $\{H=E\}$ has positive topological entropy.

title: Chaos in the symmetric ABC flow
credit: T. Dombre, U. Frisch, J. M. Greene, M. Henon, A. Mehr, A. M. Soward, 'Chaotic streamlines in the ABC flows', J. Fluid Mech. 167 (1986); V. I. Arnold (1965); M. Henon (1966).
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.17449 (Szuminski-Llibre, 2026 preprint): relied on only for the openness check (it is perturbative near the axes and does not settle A=B=C=1); the statement assumes nothing from it.
plain: The ABC flow with all three coefficients equal to 1 is the classical steady Euler flow on the 3-torus that is believed to be chaotic. Prove that it really is: show it has positive topological entropy.
math: Prove that the flow of $\dot x=\sin z+\cos y,\ \dot y=\sin x+\cos z,\ \dot z=\sin y+\cos x$ on $\mathbb{T}^3=(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^3$ has positive topological entropy (e.g. by exhibiting a transversal homoclinic orbit to a hyperbolic periodic orbit, or a horseshoe for a Poincare map).

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
credit: Belk, Hyde, Moore (2022), arXiv:2211.05825, Questions 3–4.
plain: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
math: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)

title: Ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron billiard
plain: A billiard ball bounces inside a regular tetrahedron. The tetrahedron does not tile space, and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi. So the billiard cannot be unfolded into a straight-line flow on a torus or a translation structure. Is the motion ergodic, so that almost every trajectory equidistributes in position and direction?
math: Let $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a regular tetrahedron and $\phi_t$ the billiard flow on the unit tangent bundle $T^1\Delta$, with specular reflection at faces and orbits hitting edges or vertices discarded (a null set). Prove or disprove that $\phi_t$ is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure.

title: From density to Kolmogorov typicality of positive entropy in symplectic families
credit: P. Berger and D. Turaev, arXiv:2507.11375 (2025), Thm B; P. Berger, arXiv:2003.09329 (Kolmogorov typicality / emergence).
premise_risks: arXiv:2507.11375 (Berger-Turaev, 2025 preprint, refereeing status unverified): the problem assumes its Thm B (density of families with positive metric entropy at every parameter) and borrows its definition of Kolmogorov typicality.
plain: Berger and Turaev showed that families of area-preserving surface maps having positive metric entropy at every parameter are dense among smooth families. Show this is typical, i.e. holds for a Kolmogorov-generic (prevalent) set of families, or find a robust obstruction.
math: Take Σ = 𝕋² = ℝ²/ℤ² with the standard area form. For k ≥ 1 let 𝓕_k be the space of C^∞ families (f_p)_{p∈[0,1]^k} of symplectic diffeomorphisms of 𝕋² such that every f_p has an elliptic periodic point, with the C^∞ topology on (p,x) ↦ f_p(x), and 𝓕_+ = {families with h_Leb(f_p) > 0 for Lebesgue-a.e. p}. Prove or disprove: for every k ≥ 1, 𝓕_+ contains a countable intersection of open subsets dense in 𝓕_k (Kolmogorov typicality in the sense of Berger–Turaev). ¬Claim: for some k, 𝓕_+ contains no residual subset of 𝓕_k.

title: Integrability of the egg-crate torus
credit: V. V. Kozlov, non-integrability of perturbed geodesic flows on the torus (Poincaré-Kozlov theory; 'Symmetries, Topology and Resonances in Hamiltonian Mechanics', 1996); Paternain, Taimanov for entropy obstructions
plain: Put the surface z = ε sin x sin y over a flat square torus. Show its geodesic flow is never integrable, however small the bumps are.
math: For $\varepsilon>0$ let $g_\varepsilon$ be the metric on $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ induced from the graph $z=\varepsilon\sin x\sin y$, i.e. $g_\varepsilon=dx^2+dy^2+\varepsilon^2(\cos x\sin y\,dx+\sin x\cos y\,dy)^2$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the geodesic flow on $T^*\mathbb T^2\setminus0$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of the Hamiltonian (for example, by showing positive topological entropy).

title: Is the Mandelbrot set decidable at Gaussian rationals?
credit: P. Potgieter, arXiv:cs/0604003 (2006), Sec. 2.3.
results: The reduction is correct apart from one flaw. A non-repelling cycle implies c in M, since by Fatou all cycles are repelling when c is outside M. The example arithmetic checks out: mu/2-mu^2/4=(37+16i)/100. But (*) as stated is FALSE. c=-2 and c=+-i are Gaussian-integer Misiurewicz parameters in M with all cycles repelling (c=i: 0->i->-1+i->-i->-1+i). The fix excludes Z[i], where membership is a finite check.
plain: Is there an algorithm that takes a complex number with rational real and imaginary parts and decides whether it lies in the Mandelbrot set? Escaping points can be confirmed, and so can points that have an attracting or neutral cycle of some period, since for each period that is an exact algebraic check. The trouble is points on the boundary where every cycle repels. No such Gaussian rational is known, but none has been ruled out.
math: Let $M=\{c\in\mathbb C:(f_c^{n}(0))_{n\ge0}\text{ bounded}\}$, $f_c(z)=z^2+c$. Prove or disprove that $M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ is a decidable subset of $\mathbb Q(i)$. $\mathbb Q(i)\setminus M$ is r.e. For each $n$, the existence of an $n$-cycle with multiplier of modulus $\le1$ is decidable for algebraic $c$ (Tarski), and such a cycle forces $c\in M$. $M\cap\mathbb Z[i]$ is a finite, explicitly computable set (it contains the Misiurewicz points $-2,\pm i$, whose cycles are all repelling). So a positive answer would follow from (*): every $c\in(M\cap\mathbb Q(i))\setminus\mathbb Z[i]$ has a non-repelling cycle. Prove or disprove (*). (Example: $c=(37+16i)/100$ lies on the main cardioid with multiplier $(3+4i)/5$, a Siegel parameter.)

title: Is the measure of the hyperbolic real quadratic parameters computable?
results: Checked: λ(H) is lower semicomputable. Each CE(C,γ) piece is an intersection of finite-time conditions, so it is only upper semicomputable, which is the wrong direction. The 'equivalently' clause is valid through Lyubich's regular-or-stochastic theorem and Avila–Moreira (almost every stochastic parameter is CE).
premise_risks: arXiv 2505.20495 (Golmakani–Koudjinan–Luzzatto–Pilarczyk, 2025 preprint): cited only for the remark that computer-assisted schemes certify expansion, not measure; statement does not depend on it.
plain: For real c between −2 and 1/4, the map x ↦ x²+c has an attracting cycle for an open dense set of c, yet the chaotic parameters have positive length (Jakobson). Is the total length of the parameters with an attracting cycle a computable number? It can be approximated from below by listing windows, but no known method approximates it from above.
math: Let $H=\{c\in[-2,1/4]:\ x\mapsto x^2+c\text{ has an attracting periodic orbit}\}$. Is the Lebesgue measure $\lambda(H)$ a computable real number? ($H$ is open and its components can be certified by interval arithmetic, so $\lambda(H)$ is lower semicomputable; Jakobson's theorem gives $\lambda(H)<9/4$.) Equivalently: is the measure of the set of stochastic (Collet–Eckmann) parameters lower semicomputable?

title: Outer billiards around analytic tables with flat points
credit: Moser's boundedness question (J. Moser, Stable and Random Motions, 1973); Douady (thesis, 1982); Sorrentino arXiv:2610.06418 (2026) for the C^1-generic case.
results: I checked the singularity claim. At a flat point of order k the radius of curvature satisfies rho(theta)~|theta|^{-k/(k+1)} (|theta|^{-2/3} for x^4+y^4), and the tangency point q(p) is only C^{1/(k+1)} across the tangent lines at the flat points. So T and the limiting map at infinity are genuinely non-smooth, and KAM does not apply directly. The claim is correct.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.06418 (Sorrentino, 2026 preprint): cited for C^1-generic unbounded orbits (centrally symmetric tables only); motivation only, the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Outer billiards around a smooth convex shape with positive curvature has only bounded orbits (Moser-Douady). Polygons, semicircles and generic C^1 shapes can have orbits that escape to infinity. What if the table is analytic and strictly convex, but its curvature vanishes at a few points, like the superellipse x^4+y^4 ≤ 1? Decide whether every orbit stays bounded.
math: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a strictly convex body whose boundary is a real-analytic closed curve with curvature vanishing at at least one point (hence, by analyticity, at finitely many). For $p\in\mathbb R^2\setminus K$, let $T(p)=2q-p$, where $q\in\partial K$ is the tangency point of the tangent line from $p$ that has $K$ on its left. Is every $T$-orbit bounded, for every such $K$? If not, characterize the $K$ with unbounded orbits, e.g. by the vanishing orders of the curvature or by symmetry. First test case: $K=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$.

title: Positive metric entropy for the x^4+y^4 billiard
credit: O. Knill et al., billiards in l^p unit balls (lpbilliards.pdf, Harvard); positive metric entropy for smooth convex billiards / standard-map-type problem (classical open problem)
plain: The billiard table x^4 + y^4 <= 1 is smooth and convex, but its curvature vanishes at four points, so (by Mather) it has no caustics. Its phase space mixes stable islands with apparently chaotic regions. Prove that the chaos is real: on a set of positive measure, nearby trajectories separate exponentially fast.
math:
Let $\Phi$ be the billiard map of $\Omega=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$, preserving the Liouville measure $
u=\sin	heta\,ds\,d	heta$. Prove that $h_
u(\Phi)>0$; equivalently, by Pesin's formula, that $\Phi$ has a nonzero Lyapunov exponent on a set of positive $
u$-measure.

title: Positive metric entropy of the Chirikov standard map at an explicit moderate parameter
credit: Ya. G. Sinai (conjecture, 1994); Slijepcevic 2026, arXiv:2611.09361
premise_risks: arXiv:2611.09361 (Slijepcevic, Nov 2026 preprint): the known result h_m(f_k) >= log(2 pi k+4) - 2^430 for k >= exp(2^50000), quoted as background only.
OpenAI preprint (unrefereed, credited in 2611.09361): non-effective positivity for large k, background only.
plain: Sinai conjectured that the standard map has positive metric entropy for every parameter k>0. After a 2026 AI-generated non-effective proof for large k, Slijepčević proved it for every k ≥ exp(2^{50000}). Bring the threshold down to a physically meaningful range, e.g. all k ≥ 10^6, or even a single explicit k ≤ 100.
math: Let f_k(x,y)=(x+y+k sin(2 pi x), y+k sin(2 pi x)) on T^2=R^2/Z^2 (Slijepcevic's normalization; Chirikov's K equals 2 pi k), and h_m(f_k) the metric entropy w.r.t. area. Known: log(2 pi k+4)-2^{430} <= h_m(f_k) <= log(2 pi k+4) for k>=exp(2^{50000}) (Slijepcevic 2026). Prove h_m(f_k)>0 for all k>=10^6, or for at least one explicit k<=100.

title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
credit: Borisov, Mamaev, Kilin, Regul. Chaotic Dyn. (2019); survey arXiv:2003.00716 (Thm 7); Stremler-Aref (1999, chao-dyn/9907038) for the zero-circulation integrable case
plain: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
math: For N = 3 the reduced flow on M_3 has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of H (Claim); the N = 4 analogue is a separate proposition ClaimN4, not part of Claim.

title: A monotile that forces quasicrystalline symmetry
credit: Einstein problem: Socolar-Taylor (2011, arXiv:1009.1419); Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss (2023, arXiv:2303.10798); Gummelt decagon covering (1996); Steinhardt-Jeong quasi-unit-cell model
plain: Every aperiodic monotile known (Socolar-Taylor, the hat, the spectre, and the 3D examples) has tilings with only crystallographic rotational structure: 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold. Is there a single tile in the plane whose tilings are all forced to be quasicrystalline with fivefold symmetry, as Penrose tilings are? Or is non-crystallographic symmetry something only two or more tiles can enforce?
math: Call a compact set T ⊂ ℝ² homeomorphic to a closed disc a monotile if it tiles ℝ² by isometric copies, reflections allowed. Does there exist a monotile T such that (i) every tiling by copies of T uses only finitely many orientations of T (up to translation), and (ii) for every such tiling 𝒯 the translation hull Ω(𝒯), the closure of {𝒯 + v} in the standard local topology (agreement on B(0,1/ε) after a translation of size < ε), is invariant under rotation by 2π/5? (Equivalently, the rotated tiling R𝒯 lies in Ω(𝒯).) The R³ icosahedral analogue is a secondary target.

title: A strongly aperiodic monotile in four dimensions
credit: Kamenetsky 2026, arXiv:2610.00916, Problem 9.1 (context: Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss 2023, arXiv:2303.10798; Tsiokos 2026, arXiv:2609.19214)
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.19214 (Tsiokos, 2026, unrefereed): the claimed strongly aperiodic 3D monotile Chair44 that motivates the question; Claim does not depend on it.
arXiv:2609.24779 (Goodman-Strauss, 2026, unrefereed): independent proof for Chair44; context only.
arXiv:2610.00916 (Kamenetsky, 2026, unrefereed): reports a failed 4D search and poses the problem; context only.
plain: The hat (2023) is a single shape that tiles the plane only non-periodically, and in 2026 a 3D analogue was announced (Chair44, a decorated chair-shaped polycube). Find one connected 4D shape whose copies fill 4D space, where no tiling by it is left unchanged by any translation.
math: Find a compact set $T\subset\mathbb R^4$ homeomorphic to a closed 4-ball such that (i) $\mathbb R^4$ admits a tiling by isometric copies of $T$ (reflections allowed; copies cover $\mathbb R^4$ with pairwise disjoint interiors), and (ii) no such tiling is invariant under any nonzero translation. (Drop the weak variant (ii'), or flag it as possibly easy via prisms over a 3D monotile.)

title: Beat the (1-o(1)) log2 d exponent in quasi-polynomial polytope diameter bounds
credit: Kalai-Kleitman 1992; Todd 2014 (arXiv:1402.3579); Sukegawa; Liu-Ge-Ye 2026 (arXiv:2609.33434)
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.33434 (Liu-Ge-Ye, 2026, unrefereed): the current best bound (n-d)^{log2 G_d}, G_d ~ (4 ln 2) d/(ln d)^2, and the claim that the leading term is sharp for path-counting recursions; recorded as context, Claim does not depend on it.
plain: All known bounds on the diameter of a d-dimensional polyhedron with n facets have the form (n−d)^{log₂ d − O(log log d)}. The latest (Liu–Ge–Ye 2026) is (n−d)^{log₂ G_d} with G_d ~ (4 ln 2) d/(ln d)². Get an exponent at most (1−ε) log₂ d.
math: Let $\Delta_u(d,n)$ be the maximum graph diameter of a pointed $d$-polyhedron with $n$ facets. Known: $\Delta_u(d,n)\le (n-d)^{\log_2 G_d}$, $G_d=(4\ln2+o(1))d/(\ln d)^2$ (Liu–Ge–Ye 2026), after Kalai–Kleitman, Todd, Sukegawa. Prove $\Delta_u(d,n)\le (n-d)^{(1-\varepsilon)\log_2 d}$ for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and all large $d$.

title: Cross-polytopes in 4D
credit: Klee & Wagon, Old and New Unsolved Problems in Plane Geometry and Number Theory (1991), Problem 11.5; V. V. Makeev (d = 3); R. Karasev, arXiv:0905.2671 (2009).
plain: Every smooth convex body in 4-space should have the eight corners of a regular cross-polytope lying on its boundary.
math: Prove that for every smooth convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^4$ there is a regular cross-polytope (a similar copy of $\mathrm{conv}\{\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_4\}$) all of whose 8 vertices lie on $\partial K$.

title: Geodesic squares on convex surfaces
credit: Toeplitz 1911 (square peg problem); Schnirelmann 1944 (smooth case); constant-curvature surfaces: arXiv:2507.07945 (Naseri Sadr 2025)
premise_risks: arXiv:2507.07945 (2025 preprint, refereeing unclear): results for spheres and the hyperbolic plane; context only, Claim does not depend on it.
plain: On a smooth convex surface, measure distance by the length of the shortest path on the surface. Every smooth simple closed curve on the surface should contain four points that form a 'square' in this sense: four equal sides and two equal diagonals.
math: Let $S=\partial K$ for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ with smooth boundary and positive Gaussian curvature, and let $d$ be the intrinsic distance on $S$. Prove that every smooth simple closed curve $\gamma\subset S$ contains four distinct points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, in this cyclic order along $\gamma$, with $d(p_1,p_2)=d(p_2,p_3)=d(p_3,p_4)=d(p_4,p_1)>0$ and $d(p_1,p_3)=d(p_2,p_4)$.

title: Gromov width of the 4D l^4 ball
results: c_G(U) >= pi: U contains the Euclidean unit ball, since sum x_i^4 <= (sum x_i^2)^2. (Trivial.) c_G(U) <= c_Z(U) = c_EHZ(U) = c0 = 4Gamma(5/4)^2/Gamma(3/2) ~ 3.7081 (arXiv 2609.37794, Thm 2 with n=2, p=4, B=D=I). Gromov width is <= every normalized capacity. The volume bound sqrt(2 Vol U) ~ 4.65 is weaker.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.37794 (2026, unrefereed): Thm 2 giving c_Z(U) = c_EHZ(U) = 4Γ(5/4)^2/Γ(3/2); the Claim's target value c0 comes from it. If that value is wrong, Claim may be false for a trivial reason.
plain: The 4D superball x1^4+y1^4+x2^4+y2^4 <= 1 contains the round unit ball, so it holds a symplectic ball of capacity pi. Its cylindrical capacity is about 3.708, and no symplectic ball can be bigger than that. Narrow the gap: embed a bigger ball, or show that no ball of capacity close to 3.708 fits.
math: Let U = {x1^4+y1^4+x2^4+y2^4 <= 1} ⊂ (R^4, ω0) and c_G(U) = sup{πr^2 : B^4(r) embeds symplectically in U}. Known: π <= c_G(U) <= c0 := 4Γ(5/4)^2/Γ(3/2) ≈ 3.7081 (= c_Z(U) = c_EHZ(U)). Prove or disprove: c_G(U) = c0 (i.e. U satisfies the strong Viterbo equality between Gromov width and cylindrical capacity).

title: How nearly can tetrahedra close up: the exponent
credit: Steinhaus problem; Świerczkowski (1959) non-closure; Elgersma & Wagon (2016), arXiv:1610.00280.
results: g(n) >= c*3^{-n/2} for all n (new, short proof): g_n = s_{i1}...s_{in}, linear part = ±R_q, q = v_{i1}...v_{in}, v_i the pure quaternions ±i±j±k (norm 3); non-backtracking => q primitive in the Hurwitz order (unique factorisation; checked by computer to n=11). If T_n is near T_0 the linear part is near a symmetry ±R_u; q*conj(u) cannot be real (primitivity / 2*3^n not a square), so its vector part has length >=1/2 while |q u| <= sqrt2*3^{n/2}, giving rotation error >> 3^{-n/2}.
premise_risks: QED-internal derivation (unrefereed): the bounds 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (Hurwitz-order primitivity checked by computer only to n = 11). The formal Claim only uses the definitions, not these bounds.
plain: Glue regular tetrahedra face to face in a chain of length n; it can never close exactly. How close to closing can it get? Short arguments show the best gap is at least about 3^{-n/2} and, for infinitely many n, at most about 3^{-n/12}; counting suggests 3^{-n/6}. Narrow the exponent range [1/12, 1/2].
math: Let g(k) be the minimal Hausdorff distance between T_k and T_0 over non-backtracking face-reflection chains of length k, and κ := liminf_{n→∞} −(1/n) log₃ min_{1≤k≤n} g(k). Known: 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (heuristic κ = 1/6). Prove κ > 1/12, i.e. there are δ > 0 and N such that for every n ≥ N some non-backtracking chain of length between 1 and n ends within 3^{−(1/12+δ)n} of T_0.

title: Sofa stability
credit: Baek (2024), 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa', arXiv:2411.19826.
premise_risks: arXiv:2411.19826 (Baek 2024; refereeing status unclear): the problem assumes Gerver's sofa is the maximizer. The formal Claim avoids this by quantifying over an unspecified stable sofa G, so it does not depend on Baek's result.
arXiv:2610.13955 (2026 preprint, cited in refs): context only; nothing in the statement depends on it.
plain: Baek (2024) proved that Gerver's sofa has the largest area among shapes that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1. Show that any movable sofa whose area is nearly Gerver's must be nearly Gerver's sofa in shape (which in particular gives uniqueness).
math: A moving sofa is a compact connected $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ that can be moved by a continuous rigid motion from $(-\infty,0]\times[0,1]$ to $[0,1]\times(-\infty,0]$ inside $L=((-\infty,1]\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times(-\infty,1])$. Let $G$ be Gerver's sofa, of area $A_G\approx2.21953$. Prove that there are $C,\alpha>0$ such that every moving sofa $S$ with $|S|\ge A_G-\varepsilon$ satisfies $\min_{g}|gS\,\triangle\,G|\le C\varepsilon^{\alpha}$, the minimum over rigid motions $g$ of the plane.

title: Superlinear unit distances on the unit sphere
credit: Erdős, Hickerson, Pach, 'A problem of Leo Moser about repeated distances on the sphere', Amer. Math. Monthly 96 (1989); Swanepoel-Valtr (2004)
plain: In 2026 a number-field construction showed that points in the plane can have n^(1+c) unit distances, disproving Erdos's conjecture. On a sphere of radius 1/sqrt2 an n^(4/3) construction is classical, but on the unit sphere only n·sqrt(log n) is known. Can the new ideas give a power gain there?
math: Prove or disprove: there is $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ there exist $P\subset S^2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:|x|=1\}$ with $|P|=n$ and $\#\{\{p,q\}\subset P:|p-q|=1\}\ge n^{1+c}$.

title: An explicit, checkable counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture
premise_risks: OpenAI October 2026 release (Family 157), surveyed in arXiv:2610.17090 (unrefereed): the claim that Hadwiger's conjecture is false at all. If that disproof is wrong, the problem asks for something that may not exist, and its whole motivation collapses.
arXiv:2609.35361 and arXiv:2606.01586 (2026 preprints): background on the α ≤ 2 / connected-matching route and the size of known counterexamples.
plain: Hadwiger's conjecture says a graph that needs t colours contains the complete graph K_t as a minor. A disproof claimed in October 2026 (not yet peer reviewed) is non-constructive: it uses graphs with no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, on roughly 2^(10^12) vertices or more, and never names a graph. Find one concrete graph on fewer than a million vertices for which the conjecture fails, with a proof that can be checked.
math: For a finite graph $G$ let $h(G)=\max\{t: K_t\preceq G\}$ be its Hadwiger number and $\chi(G)$ its chromatic number. Exhibit an explicit graph $G$ with $|V(G)|<10^6$ and $h(G)<\chi(G)$, with a complete proof of both bounds that can be checked (by hand or by a computer computation of feasible size). Sufficient route (Cambie): an explicit $G$ with $\alpha(G)\le2$, $|V(G)|=4t-1$ and no connected matching of size $t$ (a matching whose edges are pairwise joined by an edge of $G$) violates Hadwiger's conjecture.

title: Graceful labellings of forests
credit: Relaxation of the Ringel–Kotzig–Rosa Graceful Tree Conjecture; related: Van Bussel (EJC 2002, range-relaxed graceful labellings), Adamaszek–Allen–Grosu–Hladký arXiv:1608.01577, gracesize arXiv:2511.11331.
plain: A forest with m edges and c trees has m + c vertices. Label them with 0, 1, ..., m + c - 1, each label used once, so that the m edge differences |label(u) - label(v)| are all different. Show that every forest has such a labelling. The case 'a tree plus one isolated vertex' already says that every tree can be labelled gracefully if one spare label is allowed.
math: Prove that every forest $F$ with $m$ edges and $c\ge1$ components has a bijection $\ell:V(F)\to\{0,1,\dots,m+c-1\}$ such that the values $|\ell(u)-\ell(v)|$, $uv\in E(F)$, are pairwise distinct. (Key special case: $F=T\sqcup K_1$, i.e. every tree with $m$ edges has an injective labelling into $\{0,\dots,m+1\}$ with distinct edge differences.)

title: Ringel for forests
credit: Ringel (1963); Montgomery-Pokrovskiy-Sudakov (arXiv:2001.02665); Keevash-Staden (arXiv:2004.09947); Barrientos-Minion, EJGTA 4(2) 2016 (ρ-labelled forests)
plain: Ringel's conjecture, now a theorem for large n, says the complete graph on 2m+1 vertices splits into 2m+1 copies of any tree with m edges. Show the same holds for every forest with m edges. A stronger form asks that every such forest have a rho-labelling, which gives a cyclic decomposition.
math: Prove that for every m ≥ 1 and every forest F with m edges and no isolated vertices, E(K_{2m+1}) can be partitioned into 2m+1 subgraphs each isomorphic to F. Stronger form: every such F admits a ρ-labelling.

title: Computable connective constants
plain: Count the self-avoiding walks of length n on the Cayley graph of a finitely generated group. Their n-th roots decrease to the connective constant, so it can always be approximated from above. For groups with a solvable word problem, can it always be computed to any precision, i.e. also approximated from below?
math: Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with solvable word problem, $S=S^{-1}$ a finite generating set, $c_n$ the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks from $e$ in $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$, and $\mu(G,S)=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}=\inf_n c_n^{1/n}$ (a right-computable real). Is $\mu(G,S)$ always a computable real? If not, construct $(G,S)$ with solvable word problem and $\mu(G,S)$ non-computable. If so, is the map (word-problem algorithm, $S$) $\mapsto\mu(G,S)$ uniformly computable?

title: Deciding limit cycles
credit: Extension of Graca-Zhong (arXiv:2101.07701) noncomputability of planar periodic orbits; related: Hilbert's 16th problem, Il'yashenko on algebraic unsolvability of the center-focus problem.
results: The claim that hyperbolic limit cycles are r.e. via interval certification is correct. The remark that fixed-degree versions 'can become trivially decidable' is wrong. Each fixed-degree set is still infinite. Bautin's finite generation only gives non-uniform decidability of the local center condition, not of whether cycles exist.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.22058 (2026 preprint): cited only for the claim that the planar (N=2) case is open and that Lyapunov stability is undecidable in dimension 5; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Given a polynomial vector field in the plane with rational coefficients, is there an algorithm that decides whether it has a limit cycle, that is, an isolated closed orbit? Hilbert's 16th problem asks how many limit cycles there can be. This asks only whether their existence is algorithmically decidable. The same question can be asked for closed orbits of any kind, including those in period annuli around centres.
math: Let $\mathcal L=\{(P,Q)\in\mathbb Q[x,y]^2:\ \dot x=P,\dot y=Q$ has a limit cycle, i.e. a non-constant periodic orbit that has a neighbourhood containing no other periodic orbit$\}$ and $\mathcal P=\{(P,Q):$ the system has a non-constant periodic orbit in $\mathbb R^2\}$, with inputs given by their rational coefficient lists (degree unbounded). (a) Is $\mathcal L$ decidable? (b) Is $\mathcal P$ decidable? (c) Are $\mathcal L,\mathcal P$ or their complements recursively enumerable? (d) Same questions restricted to degree 2.

title: First-order convergence law for random Latin squares
results: Caution: route (i) as originally proposed has a flaw. The extension property 'every finite partial configuration extends in every consistent way w.h.p.' is false. A new x with x∘a1=b1 and x∘a2=b2 has expected count n·n^{-2}→0, because x∘a=b already determines x. The structure is functionally sparse (Lynch-type), not G(n,1/2)-type, so the route was rewritten.
premise_risks: arXiv:2606.18174 (Allsop-Morris, 2026 preprint): cited only as evidence that even the Poisson(1) idempotent law is unproved; the statement assumes nothing from it.
plain: Pick a Latin square of order n uniformly at random and read it as a multiplication table x∘y on n symbols. Does every first-order statement about this table have a limiting probability as n grows? A zero-one law fails: the number of x with x∘x=x should be asymptotically Poisson(1), so the probability that one exists should tend to 1−1/e rather than 0 or 1.
math: Let $L_n$ be uniform among Latin squares on $[n]$ and $\mathcal Q_n=([n],\circ)$ with $x\circ y=L_n(x,y)$. Prove or disprove: for every first-order sentence $\varphi$ in the language $\{\circ,=\}$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr[\mathcal Q_n\models\varphi]$ exists. (A 0-1 law should fail: by symbol-relabelling symmetry, $\mathbb E\#\{x:x\circ x=x\}=1$ exactly, and this count is conjecturally Poisson(1).) Expected route, as for Lynch's random unary functions: (i) w.h.p. the bounded-depth term closure of any bounded tuple is free except for coincidences counted by balanced configurations ($v$ elements, $v$ independent equations); (ii) a joint Poisson limit for the counts of all such balanced configurations, e.g. cycles of $x\mapsto x\circ x$. A disproof would need a definable sparse statistic with no limit law.

title: Hat Ising universality
credit: Hat tiling: Smith, Myers, Kaplan, Goodman-Strauss (2023); numerics on hat-tiling Ising models as cited in the notes (arXiv:2402.11331, arXiv:2307.11054); background: Chelkak-Smirnov universality on isoradial graphs.
plain: Magnets on a hat tiling should behave at their critical point exactly like magnets on a square grid. Prove it.
math: Let T be any hat tiling (tiling of ℂ by isometric copies, reflections allowed, of the Smith–Myers–Kaplan–Goodman-Strauss hat; all such tilings form the hull) and G its tile-adjacency graph (tiles sharing a boundary segment), with the J=1 ferromagnetic Ising model. Prove: there is β_c ∈ (0,∞), the same for all T, such that, with constants c, C, δ > 0 depending only on T: (a) the plus-state magnetization M_T(β,x) = 0 for all tiles x and 0 ≤ β ≤ β_c, and c(β−β_c)^{1/8} ≤ M_T(β,x) ≤ C(β−β_c)^{1/8} uniformly in x for β_c < β < β_c+δ; (b) for β_c−δ < β < β_c, χ_T(β) = sup_x Σ_y ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩_β satisfies c(β_c−β)^{−7/4} ≤ χ_T(β) ≤ C(β_c−β)^{−7/4}; (c) for β_c−δ < β < β_c, the inverse correlation length 1/ξ_T(β) = liminf_{|x−y|→∞} (−log⟨σ_xσ_y⟩_β/|x−y|) satisfies c(β_c−β) ≤ 1/ξ_T(β) ≤ C(β_c−β).

title: Irrationality of the quartic oscillator ground state
plain: The lowest energy of the quartic oscillator, -d^2/dx^2 + x^4 on the line, is about 1.0603620905. Show that it is irrational.
math: Let $E_0=\min\sigma\big(-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}+x^4\big)$, the operator taken self-adjoint on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ ($E_0=1.06036209048418\ldots$). Prove that $E_0\notin\mathbb Q$.

title: Spikes at the squares
credit: Cheon, Exner, Šeba (2000), arXiv:quant-ph/0004058 (continuum analogue with spikes at the squares).
results: Correct with a caveat. The spike gaps are 2m+1, so the spike-to-spike map is C·R(k(2m+1)), a one-frequency analytic cocycle over rotation by 2k. Herman's subharmonicity gives L ≥ log|C_11| = log sqrt(1+λ²/(4sin²k)). This bounds the phase-averaged exponent only: at the fixed phase θ=k (coupled to the frequency) the limit is not guaranteed, so eigenfunction decay is heuristic.
plain: On the half-line lattice, add a fixed spike of height λ at every perfect square. The free band (-2,2) then has no absolutely continuous spectrum, by Remling's theorem. Decide whether the spectrum inside the band is pure point (localized states) or singular continuous. A heuristic in the physics literature predicts singular continuous.
math: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\,\mathbf 1_{\{m^2:m\ge1\}}(n)\,u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$ fixed, and let $\mu$ be the spectral measure of $\delta_1$. Determine the spectral type of $\mu|_{(-2,2)}$: is it pure point, purely singular continuous, or mixed? (Known: $\mu_{ac}=0$ by Remling's theorem. Cheon–Exner–Šeba heuristically predict purely singular continuous spectrum for the continuum analogue; positive Lyapunov exponents of the spike-to-spike cocycle suggest pure point.)

title: Ten Martini for every periodic planar lattice
credit: Extends Avila–Jitomirskaya (Ten Martini, Annals 2009) and Becker–Han–Jitomirskaya–Zworski (honeycomb, arXiv:1803.00988).
results: The pendant-twin counterexample is correct. Attach two pendant vertices x,x' to each vertex of Z^2. Then delta_x - (phase) delta_x' is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0 for every B. For E nonzero, E is in sigma iff E-2/E is in sigma(H_sq), which lies in [-4,4]. So a punctured neighbourhood of 0 is a gap, 0 is isolated, and the naive statement fails.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.15812 (2026 preprint): 1D Robust Ten Martini; cited as a possible tool only, M does not depend on it.
arXiv:2611.10767 (2026 preprint): cited; M does not depend on it.
plain: A tight-binding electron on any doubly periodic planar network in a uniform magnetic field: is the energy spectrum always a Cantor set when the flux per cell is irrational? This is known for the square lattice (Ten Martini), the honeycomb lattice and the Lieb lattice, each by a reduction to a one-dimensional operator. Flat-band eigenvalues that persist in any field can sit isolated, so they must be set aside. The question is whether what remains is always a Cantor set, or at least never contains an interval.
math: Let $G\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a connected planar graph with straight edges that is invariant under a lattice $L\cong\mathbb Z^2$ and has finitely many $L$-orbits of vertices. For a constant field $B$ with vector potential $A$, set $(H_B\psi)(x)=\sum_{y\sim x}e^{i\int_{[x,y]}A}\psi(y)$ on $\ell^2(V(G))$, and let $2\pi\alpha=B\cdot\mathrm{covol}(L)$. Let $\Sigma'$ be the derived set of $\sigma(H_B)$, i.e. $\sigma(H_B)$ minus its isolated points (eigenvalues of infinite multiplicity, i.e. flat bands). Prove or disprove: for every such $G$ and every irrational $\alpha$, $\Sigma'$ is a nonempty Cantor set. At minimum, decide whether $\sigma(H_B)$ is always nowhere dense. The first open instance is the kagome lattice in a uniform field. (The pure line-graph flux pattern, with no flux through the triangles, reduces to the honeycomb case.)

title: Break the 5/8 barrier for primes with triply well-factorable weights
credit: A. Pascadi, arXiv:2505.00653 (2025), Thm 1.3 and remarks on the 5/8 limit; J. D. Lichtman, arXiv:2309.08522 (2023); triply well-factorable weights from Maynard's equidistribution papers.
premise_risks: arXiv:2505.00653 (Pascadi, 2025 preprint, refereeing status unverified): the known baseline θ* ≥ 5/8 unconditionally and the exact definition of triply well-factorable weights (Def 1.1) are taken from it.
arXiv:2602.20917 and arXiv:2608.13299 (2026 preprints): used only to check that no one has passed 5/8; the statement assumes nothing from them.
plain: The primes are known to be evenly spread over residue classes, on average over moduli up to x^{5/8}, if the average is weighted by triply well-factorable weights. Push the exponent past 5/8, or show the dispersion method cannot.
math: Say (lambda_q)_{q<=Q} is triply well-factorable of level Q if for all Q1Q2Q3=Q there are 1-bounded alpha,beta,gamma supported on q_i<=Q_i with lambda=alpha*beta*gamma (Dirichlet convolution). Let theta* = sup of theta such that for all eps,A>0, fixed a!=0, and every such lambda of level Q=x^{theta-eps}: sum_{q<=Q,(q,a)=1} lambda_q(pi(x;q,a)-pi(x)/phi(q)) <<_{eps,A,a} x(log x)^{-A}. Known theta*>=5/8 (Pascadi). Prove theta*>5/8.

title: Close the gap in the density of integers that are sums of two rational cubes
credit: Alpöge, Bhargava, Shnidman, Integers expressible as the sum of two rational cubes, arXiv:2210.10730 (2022); Koymans-Smith arXiv:2606.06024 (2026) for the complement side.
premise_risks: arXiv:2606.06024 (Koymans-Smith, 2026 preprint): source of the 31.95% (0.3195) lower bound for non-sums; the formalized Claim does not use it, but the stated M does.
plain: BSD plus the minimalist rank heuristic predict that exactly half of all integers are sums of two rational cubes. Proven: at least 2/21 are (Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman), and at least 31.95% are not (Koymans–Smith). Improve either bound.
math: Let $\mathcal S=\{n\in\mathbb Z: n=x^3+y^3,\ x,y\in\mathbb Q\}$ and $d_\pm$ the lower densities of $\mathcal S$ and of its complement (ordered by $|n|$). Known: $\underline d(\mathcal S)\ge 2/21$, $\underline d(\mathcal S^c)\ge 0.3195$. Conjecture: both densities equal $1/2$. Improve either constant.

title: Do GRH and Elliott–Halberstam together refute the Alternative Hypothesis?
credit: Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya, Turnage-Butterbaugh, The Alternative Hypothesis for zeros of the Riemann zeta-function, arXiv:2508.10857 (2025); Goldston et al., arXiv:2507.06823; Lagarias–Rodgers arXiv:1905.12123.
premise_risks: arXiv:2508.10857 (2025 preprint, unrefereed as far as known): the problem takes its precise definition of AH, and the claimed explicit limit of F(α) under RH + AH, from this paper.
arXiv:2507.06823 (2025 preprint): background on F(α) under AH.
plain: The Alternative Hypothesis says normalized gaps between zeta zeros are almost all near half-integers. It contradicts GUE, but no proven hypothesis is known to rule it out. Decide whether GRH plus Elliott–Halberstam (strong statements about primes, not zeros) is incompatible with it.
math: Let AH be as in arXiv:2508.10857. Does RH + GRH for Dirichlet L-functions + the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (or GEH) imply that AH fails? (The 'equivalently' clause is a research route, not an equivalent statement, and is dropped.)

title: Improve H_1 <= 12 under EH alone
credit: D.H.J. Polymath 2014, arXiv:1407.4897; J. Maynard 2015, arXiv:1311.4600
plain: Assuming Elliott–Halberstam, Maynard's sieve gives infinitely many pairs of primes at distance at most 12. The generalized conjecture GEH gives 6. Lower 12 using EH alone.
math: Let $H_1=\liminf_{n}(p_{n+1}-p_n)$. Assuming EH (level $\theta=1-\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon>0$, for the von Mangoldt function only, not GEH), prove $H_1\le 10$, or prove that no Selberg/Maynard-type sieve weight using EH alone can give $H_1<12$.

title: Interval-sieve extremal bounds behind the Banks–Ford–Tao gap prediction
credit: Banks, Ford, Tao, Large prime gaps and probabilistic models, Invent. Math. 2023 (arXiv:1908.08613)
plain: Banks, Ford and Tao showed that a random sieve model of the primes predicts the largest prime gap below x is about g(ξ log²x), where g is controlled by an extremal sieve quantity W_y. W_y is the fewest survivors in [0,y] after one residue class is removed for each prime up to √(y/log y). Narrow the bounds on W_y.
math: Let W_y = min over residue choices (a_p) of #{n ∈ [0,y] ∩ ℤ : n ≢ a_p (mod p) for all primes p <= (y/log y)^{1/2}}. Known (Banks-Ford-Tao): (4+o(1)) y log log y/log^2 y <= W_y <= y/log y + O(y log log y/log^2 y). Prove or disprove: there is an absolute c > 0 with W_y >= c·y/log y for all sufficiently large y.

title: Largest prime factor of Markov numbers
credit: Extends Corvaja–Zannier, 'On the greatest prime factor of Markov pairs', Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova 116 (2006).
plain: Markov numbers are the numbers appearing in positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Show that the largest prime factor of a Markov number tends to infinity. Equivalently, for any finite set of primes, only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
math: Let $\mathcal M=\{m\ge1:\exists\,x,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ x^2+y^2+m^2=3xym\}$ and let $P(m)$ denote the largest prime factor of $m$ (with $P(1)=1$). Prove that $P(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ in $\mathcal M$; equivalently, for every finite set $S$ of primes, only finitely many $m\in\mathcal M$ are $S$-units.

title: Lower the exponent 0.7785 for A4-quartic fields
credit: Bhargava, Shankar, Taniguchi, Thorne, Tsimerman, Zhao, 'Bounds on 2-torsion in class groups of number fields and integral points on elliptic curves', JAMS 2020 (arXiv:1701.02458, Thm 1.4); Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248
premise_risks: arXiv:2510.05248 (Loughran-Paterson, 2025 preprint): lower bound X^{1/2} log X and the statement that 0.7784... is the current record; the Claim itself depends only on the refereed BSTTTZ exponent.
arXiv:2602.23619 (Alberts-Bucur, 2026 preprint): cited only for the status 'no 2026 improvement'.
plain: Malle predicts about X^{1/2} log X quartic fields with Galois group A4 and discriminant up to X. Loughran–Paterson (2025) proved the matching lower bound. The best upper bound is still about X^{0.7785}. Lower the exponent.
math: Let N_{A4}(X) count quartic L/Q with Gal(L~/Q)=A4 and |Delta_L|<=X. Known: X^{1/2} log X << N_{A4}(X) << X^{0.7784...+eps} (Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248 Thm 1.1; BSTTTZ JAMS 2020 Thm 1.4). Prove N_{A4}(X) << X^{beta} for some beta<0.7784 (ideally beta=1/2+eps).

title: Lower the exponent 1/2 in Pasten's subexponential abc bound
credit: Extends H. Pasten, Invent. Math. 2024 (arXiv:2312.03566), Thm 1.4.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.01327 (2026 preprint): cited in refs; M does not depend on it.
plain: Unconditionally, abc is known only in very weak forms. Pasten (2024) proved that if a ≤ c^{1−η} then log c ≤ η^{-1} exp(κ√(log R · log log R)), with R = rad(abc). abc predicts log c ≤ (1+ε) log R + O(1). Replace the square root by any smaller power of log R.
math: For coprime $a+b=c$ with $R=\mathrm{rad}(abc)$, Pasten (Invent. Math. 2024, Thm 1.4) proves: if $a\le c^{1-\eta}$ then $\log c\le \eta^{-1}\exp\big(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\,\log_2 R}\big)$; and $\log c\le q\exp(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\log_2R})$ with $q=\min\{P(a),P(b),P(c)\}$. Prove either statement with $\exp((\log R)^{\theta})$ for some fixed $\theta<1/2$, or $\exp(O(\sqrt{\log R}))$.

title: One-level density of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions beyond support (−2,2)
credit: Özlük–Snyder (Canad. J. Math. 58, 2006; earlier 1999 work) and Rubinstein (Duke 2001) for support (−2,2); Katz–Sarnak (1999) density conjectures.
plain: Under GRH, the low-lying zeros of L(s,χ_d) for quadratic characters are known to follow the symplectic random-matrix law only for test functions whose Fourier transform is supported in (−2,2). Go beyond 2.
math: For the family of real primitive characters $\chi_{8d}$, $d$ odd squarefree, $X<d\le 2X$, and even Schwartz $\phi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\hat\phi\subset(-\sigma,\sigma)$, prove under GRH that $\frac1{|\mathcal F|}\sum_d\sum_{\gamma_d}\phi\!\big(\gamma_d\frac{\log X}{2\pi}\big)\to\int\phi(x)\big(1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\big)dx$ for some $\sigma>2$.

title: Push the GRH lower bound for Montgomery's F(alpha) beyond alpha = 1
credit: Goldston, Gonek, Özlük, Snyder (2000), 'On the pair correlation of zeros of the Riemann zeta-function', Proc. London Math. Soc.
plain: Montgomery's function F(α) is known only for |α|≤1 (on RH). Under GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder proved F(α) ≥ 3/2−|α|−ε on 1≤|α|≤3/2, while the conjecture says F(α)=1 there. Improve this lower bound.
math: Assume GRH for all Dirichlet $L$-functions. Prove that for some $\delta>0$ and all $\alpha\in[1,1+\delta]$, $\liminf_{T\to\infty}F(\alpha,T)\ge \tfrac32-\alpha+\delta$, or prove $\liminf_T \int_{1}^{3/2}F(\alpha,T)\,d\alpha>1/8$ (the value forced by the GGOS bound).

title: Second moment of 3-torsion in imaginary quadratic class groups
credit: Cohen, Lenstra, 'Heuristics on class groups of number fields', LNM 1068 (1984); Davenport-Heilbronn (1971) for the first moment
plain: Davenport–Heilbronn showed the average of |Cl(K)[3]| over imaginary quadratic fields is 2, as Cohen–Lenstra predicts. Cohen–Lenstra also predict the average of |Cl(K)[3]|² is 6. Prove this, or at least that the average is bounded.
math: Let $K$ range over imaginary quadratic fields with $|D_K|<X$. Cohen–Lenstra ($\mathbb E\,\#\mathrm{Sur}(\mathrm{Cl}_K,H)=1$ for $H=(\mathbb Z/3)^2$) predict $\frac{1}{\#\{K\}}\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\to 6$. Prove this limit, or prove $\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\ll X$.

title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
plain: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
math: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.

title: Blow-up under a steady force
credit: Fefferman, Clay Millennium problem statement (forced breakdown on R^3); OpenAI forced blow-up claim (2026, unrefereed)
premise_risks: OpenAI company PDF (cdn.openai.com navier-stokes.pdf, unrefereed): claimed time-dependent forced blow-up. This is motivation only and Claim does not depend on it.
arXiv:2609.10262 (2026 preprint): cited for context (possibly the source of the Cao-Chi-Nie gradient-force remark); Claim does not depend on it.
plain: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a push that varies in time and is switched on and off. Can a smooth, compactly supported push that never changes in time also drive a fluid at rest to a singularity?
math:
Decide whether there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, independent of $t$, such that the solution of $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=\Delta u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ loses smoothness in finite time.

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
credit: Extension of Weinstein (Comm. Math. Phys. 1983) mass-critical threshold; related Strichartz work on flat cones by Ford and by Blair-Ford-Marzuola.
plain: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
math: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global (forward-in-time) $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time (its $H^1$ norm is unbounded on its maximal interval $[0,T)$, $T<\infty$). (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)

title: Derivative loss in L4 Strichartz on the cube surface
credit: Blair, Ford, Marzuola, Strichartz estimates for the wave equation on flat cones / Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, arXiv:1003.0666.
results: s* >= 0 (trivial). No positive lower bound known. s* <= 1/4: Blair-Ford-Marzuola, Thm 1.5 (arXiv 1003.0666), loss 1/p for compact Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, p=q=4; authors call the loss an artifact of the method.
plain: On the flat torus, the L4 space-time estimate for Schrodinger waves loses only epsilon derivatives (Bourgain). On the surface of a cube, which has eight cone points that diffract waves, only a loss of 1/4 derivative is known. Find the true loss: prove any loss below 1/4, or show some loss is necessary.
math: Let $S$ be the unit cube surface, $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\text{vertices})$, and $s^*=\inf\{s\ge0:\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_s\|f\|_{H^s(S)}\}$. Known: $0\le s^*\le\tfrac14$ (Blair–Ford–Marzuola). Prove $s^*<\tfrac14$, or $s^*>0$; ideally determine $s^*$ (conjecturally $0$). The board's target (Claim) is $s^*<\tfrac14$.

title: Does an oscillating source lower the Strauss exponent?
results: Bound p_c<=1+sqrt2 is correct: John/Zhou iteration uses only |F(u)|<=C|u|^p and |F(u)-F(v)|<=C(|u|+|v|)^{p-1}|u-v|, both hold for g(t)|u|^p. The 'resonance predicts 2' heuristic (exp of int t^{1-p}) is arithmetically right but not an argument; a normal-form attempt (H''=g) just recycles the oscillating factor, so nothing is proved.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.28389 (2026 preprint): cited background on Strauss-type problems with time-dependent coefficients; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: For the 3D wave equation with source |u|^p, small smooth data give global solutions exactly when p > 1+√2 (Strauss). Multiply the source by a factor that oscillates periodically in time with average zero, such as cos t. The global-existence proof still works above 1+√2. Every blow-up proof below it breaks, because they all need the source to be positive. Is the true threshold strictly smaller?
math: For u_tt − Δu = cos(t)|u|^p on R^{1+3} (continuous Kirchhoff–Duhamel mild solutions), is p_c < 1+√2, i.e. does some p in (1,1+√2) have small-data global existence for all real C_c^∞ data? Exact p_c, dependence on g and lifespan are not formalized; the all-g version is ClaimGeneral (secondary).

premise_risks: arXiv:2602.13963 (2026 preprint, cited in refs): background on 1D/sign-of-stretching models only; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Flip the sign of the vortex-stretching term in the 3D Euler vorticity equation and keep advection and the Biot-Savart law. Do smooth solutions stay smooth forever, or can they blow up in finite time?

title: Forced blow-up up to the Lions threshold
credit: OpenAI, forced Navier–Stokes blow-up (Sep 2026, unrefereed PDF); Lions (1969) for α ≥ 5/4; Tao, averaged Navier–Stokes (arXiv:1402.0290).
premise_risks: OpenAI Navier–Stokes PDF (Sep 2026, company PDF, unrefereed, reportedly Lean-formalized): the problem assumes forced blow-up from rest is known at α = 1.
arXiv:2609.10262 (2026 preprint): cited as related forced-blow-up work for the Laplacian; motivation only.
plain: With an ordinary Laplacian, a smooth compactly supported push can make a fluid at rest blow up in finite time (OpenAI, 2026). With dissipation (-Δ)^α for α ≥ 5/4, Lions proved that solutions stay smooth. Does forced blow-up from rest still happen for every α strictly between 1 and 5/4?

In particular, is it all of $(1,5/4)$, or is it nonempty?

title: Forced Navier–Stokes blow-up at a no-slip wall
credit: Extends the OpenAI 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up (cdn.openai.com navier-stokes.pdf) and Cao–Chi–Nie, arXiv:2609.10262.
premise_risks: OpenAI navier-stokes.pdf (company PDF, unrefereed): the existence of forced finite-time blow-up on R^3/T^3 from rest with C_c^infty force; motivates the problem (statement itself does not depend on it).
Cao–Chi–Nie arXiv:2609.10262 (2026 preprint): interior-ball placement of blow-up in domains; used to argue interior case is 'already available'.
Lei–Ren arXiv:2609.35406 (2026 preprint): R^3 forced blow-up; background only.
plain: In 2026 it was shown that a smooth, compactly supported force can drive the 3D Navier–Stokes equations, started from rest, to blow up in finite time. Inside a domain this can simply be copied away from any wall. Show that blow-up can also happen at the wall itself: in a half-space with the no-slip condition, the velocity becomes unbounded at a point of the boundary.

title: Heat with a cosine reaction
credit: H. Fujita 1966 (critical exponent); R. Pinsky 1997 (weighted Fujita problem, a >= 0)
plain: In u_t = u_xx + cos(x) u^2 the reaction term averages to zero over a period, but a second-order (homogenization) effect produces an effective +u^3 term, which in one dimension is exactly Fujita's borderline exponent where every positive solution of u_t = u_xx + u^3 blows up. Does every positive solution of the cosine equation blow up in finite time?
math: Let $d\ge1$, $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ be $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic with $\int_{[0,1]^d}a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$. Consider $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$, $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$. Prove: (i) if $1<p\le1+1/d$, every such solution blows up in finite time; (ii) if $p>1+1/d$, solutions with sufficiently small $u_0$ are global. Test case: $d=1$, $p=2$, $a=\cos(2\pi x)$ (equivalently $a=\cos x$ with $2\pi$-periodicity).

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
plain: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
math: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.

title: Liouville theorem for Lane-Emden with a shifted nonlinearity
plain: Gidas-Spruck: -Delta u = u^p has no positive solution on R^n for subcritical p. Replace u^p by the value of u^p at a shifted point x+e. Is there still no positive solution, for every subcritical p?
math: Let $n\ge3$, $1<p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$, $e\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Prove or disprove: there is no positive $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)$ with $-\Delta u(x)=u(x+e)^p$ for all $x$. (For $1<p<\frac n{n-2}$ the standard Mitidieri–Pohozaev test-function argument applies, since the shift is negligible at large scales; the open range is $\frac n{n-2}\le p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$. One may also ask whether positive solutions exist for $p\ge\frac{n+2}{n-2}$.)

title: Mass-critical scattering on flat cones
credit: B. Dodson, global well-posedness and scattering for the defocusing L^2-critical NLS in d=2 (Duke Math. J. 2016)
results: Both trivial cases check out. For alpha=2pi/k, C_alpha=R^2/Z_k: the Friedrichs modes e^{ikmθ} with Bessel order k|m| match the Z_k-invariant plane functions, and Dodson applies for any mass, with mass scaled by k. For radial data the m=0 mode on the cone is the 2D radial Laplacian. The sign convention iu_t+Δu=+|u|^2u is defocusing.
plain: Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrodinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Prove the same on every flat cone, a plane with a single conical singularity of total angle alpha. For alpha = 2pi/k it follows from Dodson by symmetry, and radial data are also easy. Every other angle, such as the surface of a cube corner (alpha = 3pi/2) or alpha > 2pi, is open.
math: For $\alpha>0$ let $\mathcal C_\alpha=(0,\infty)\times(\mathbb R/\alpha\mathbb Z)$ with metric $dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$ and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $C_c^\infty(\mathcal C_\alpha)$. Prove that for every $\alpha>0$ and every $u_0\in L^2(\mathcal C_\alpha)$ the solution of $iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$, $u(0)=u_0$, is global with $\|u\|_{L^4_{t,x}(\mathbb R\times\mathcal C_\alpha)}<\infty$, hence scatters in $L^2$. (Known: $\alpha=2\pi/k$, since $\mathcal C_{2\pi/k}=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z_k$ and Dodson applies to $\mathbb Z_k$-invariant data. Radial data for any $\alpha$, since the radial equation coincides with the 2D one.)

title: Quintic Szego growth
credit: Gérard–Grellier (cubic Szegő equation, turbulent solutions); Thirouin, quadratic Szegő equation (arXiv:1710.01512).
plain: The cubic Szego equation on the circle is completely integrable, and Gerard-Grellier showed that its smooth solutions can have Sobolev norms that are unbounded in time. Decide whether the quintic Szego equation, which is presumably not integrable, also has smooth solutions with unbounded high Sobolev norms.
math: On $L^2_+(\mathbb T)=\{u\in L^2:\hat u(k)=0\ \forall k<0\}$ with Szego projector $\Pi$, consider $i\partial_tu=\Pi(|u|^4u)$, which is globally well posed in $H^s_+$, $s>1/2$, with conserved $\|u\|_{L^2}$, $(Du,u)$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}$. Decide whether there exist $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)\cap L^2_+$ and $s>1/2$ with $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$.

title: Ising spin at a cube corner
credit: Chelkak, Hongler, Izyurov, Conformal invariance of spin correlations in the planar Ising model, Ann. Math. 2015 (arXiv:1202.2838)
results: The CFT step is correct. With w=z^{4/3}, the apex spin has dimension (2pi/alpha)(1/8)=1/6, and 1/6+1/8=7/24. For alpha=2pi the formula gives back 1/4. The lattice description is right: the apex has degree 3 and axis vertices have degree 4. The beta_c value is right. The free-boundary infinite-volume limit exists by GKS monotonicity. The apex defect is irrelevant (energy dimension >0), so 7/24 should be universal.
plain: Glue three quarter-planes of the square grid into the surface of an infinite cube corner (a flat cone of angle 3π/2) and run the critical Ising model. Prove that the spin at the corner decorrelates with the exponent 7/24 predicted by conformal field theory.
math: Let $\Gamma$ be the union of the three quadrant lattices $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2$ on the faces of $\partial\mathbb R_{\ge0}^3$, glued along the coordinate axes, with apex $o$ (degree 3; every other vertex has degree 4). Let $\langle\cdot\rangle$ be the infinite-volume limit of the nearest-neighbour Ising model at $\beta_c=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$ with free boundary conditions on $\Gamma\cap\{\|x\|_\infty\le n\}$. Prove $\langle\sigma_o\sigma_x\rangle\asymp|x|^{-7/24}$ as $|x|\to\infty$.

title: Alternating quotients of knot groups
credit: Dunfield-Thurston, Finite covers of random 3-manifolds, Invent. Math. 2006 (arXiv:math/0502567), question on alternating quotients; Everitt / Liebeck-Shalev for Fuchsian groups
results: Computer-verified in a fresh script: trefoil (xyx=yxy) surjects onto A5 but not A6 or A7. Figure-eight (w=x^-1yxy^-1) surjects onto A4 and A6 but not A5, A7 or A8, and has no S3 quotient, as det=5 requires. n>=9 not rerun (would take more than 30s). The trefoil argument (centre maps trivially, factor through C2*C3, Miller's (2,3)-generation) is correct.
plain: The trefoil's group maps onto every alternating group A_n with n>=9, because modulo its centre it is the modular group. Show that every nontrivial knot group maps onto A_n for all large n, or at least for infinitely many n, and bound the last exception in terms of the knot.
math: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot and $G_K=\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$. (a) Prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for all $n\ge N(K)$, and bound $N(K)$ in terms of the crossing number. (b) Weaker: prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for infinitely many $n$, or even for one $n\ge5$. Data (exhaustive search over pairs of conjugate even permutations, meridians $x,y$ with $wx=yw$): for the trefoil ($w=xy$) a surjection exists exactly for $n=5$ and $n\ge9$, since every surjection kills the centre and factors through $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\cong C_2*C_3$, and Miller proved $(2,3)$-generation of $A_n$ for $n\ne3,6,7,8$. For the figure-eight knot ($w=x^{-1}yxy^{-1}$) a surjection exists for $n=6,9,10$ and not for $n=5,7,8$. Is $N(4_1)=9$, i.e. does $G_{4_1}$ surject onto $A_n$ for every $n\ge9$?

title: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
credit: Etnyre & Ghrist (2000), arXiv:math-ph/9906021; Enciso, Peralta-Salas (and Romaniega), arXiv:2006.15033.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.17449 (Szumiński–Llibre, 2026 preprint): cited only as related perturbative work; nothing in the statement depends on it.
plain: Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines, and generic high-frequency Beltrami fields on the torus contain every knot. Show that the most-studied explicit example, the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1, has closed streamlines tied in infinitely many different knots.
math: Let $X=(\sin z+\cos y,\ \sin x+\cos z,\ \sin y+\cos x)$ on $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ (a curl eigenfield, $\nabla\times X=X$). Prove that the periodic orbits of $X$ that lie in some embedded 3-ball $B\subset\mathbb T^3$ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in $B\cong$ a ball in $\mathbb R^3$). Stronger: every knot type is realized.

title: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
credit: Extends Jones–Przytycki (Lissajous knots and billiard knots, 1998) and Koseleff–Pecker, 'Every knot is a billiard knot', arXiv:1106.5600; periodic orbits in polyhedra: Bedaride–Rao arXiv:1104.1051.
plain: A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, without hitting edges or corners, traces a closed polygon in space. Is any such polygon knotted, and do infinitely many different knot types occur?
math: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of $T$ and its image is an embedded closed polygon. (a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite.

title: Galois groups of Keller fibers
plain: Gallagher (2026) built, for every n>=3, a polynomial map C^3->C^3 with constant nonzero Jacobian whose general fibre has exactly n points. Determine the symmetry (monodromy/Galois) group of how those n points are permuted.
math: Let $H_n:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ be Gallagher's Keller map of geometric degree $n$ (A. Gallagher, \emph{An infinite family of counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension three}, Zenodo 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21479195), so $[\mathbb C(x,y,z):H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)]=n$. For each $n\ge3$ determine the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x,y,z)/H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)$ (equivalently the monodromy group of the $n$-sheeted covering over a general point), as a permutation group of degree $n$; and the arithmetic group over $\mathbb Q$.

title: Keller maps injective on integer points
plain: Take a polynomial map of 3-space with integer coefficients whose Jacobian determinant is identically 1 (a Keller map). Show that if it never sends two different integer points to the same point, then it is a polynomial automorphism.
math: Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y,z]^3$ with $\det JF\equiv 1$. Prove that if $F|_{\mathbb{Z}^3}$ is injective, then $F$ has a polynomial inverse (equivalently, by Bia{\l}ynicki-Birula--Rosenlicht, $F$ is injective on $\mathbb{C}^3$).

title: Keller monodromy is everything
plain: Since 2026 there are polynomial maps of 3-space with constant nonzero Jacobian that are not invertible (counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture), and every number n >= 3 of points in a generic fibre occurs. Show that for every n the fibre points can be permuted in every possible way by going around loops, i.e. the monodromy group can be the full symmetric group S_n.
math: Prove that for every $n\ge3$ there is a polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, of geometric degree $[\mathbb C(x):\mathbb C(F)]=n$, whose geometric monodromy group (the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x_1,x_2,x_3)/\mathbb C(F_1,F_2,F_3)$, acting on the $n$ generic fibre points) is $S_n$.

title: Closed-form Euler blow-up
plain: Smooth compactly supported starting data for the 3D Euler equations that blow up in finite time are now known to exist, but the construction is an infinite iterative series. Give such data as an explicit formula.
math: Find an explicit divergence-free $u_0=\nabla\times\big(P(x)e^{-|x|^2}\big)$ with $P\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,x_3]^3$ (or another explicitly specified finite closed-form class) such that the unforced 3D incompressible Euler solution on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $u(0)=u_0$ has finite maximal smooth lifespan.

title: Drum tones of superellipses
plain: Take the region |x|^p + |y|^p <= r^p, scaled to have area 1. At p = 2 it is a disk, which has the lowest possible bass note of any region of that area (Faber–Krahn). As p grows to infinity it becomes a square, whose note is higher. Show that the note rises steadily the whole way from p = 2 to infinity.
math: For $p\in[2,\infty)$ let $D_p=\{(x,y):|x|^p+|y|^p\le r_p^p\}$ with $r_p$ chosen so that $|D_p|=1$, and let $\lambda_1(p)$ be the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-\Delta$ on $D_p$. Prove that $\lambda_1$ is strictly increasing on $[2,\infty)$, with $\lambda_1(2)=\pi j_{0,1}^2$ and $\lambda_1(p)\uparrow2\pi^2$ as $p\to\infty$.

title: Multiplicities on the Fermat quartic
plain: The surface x^4+y^4+z^4 = 1 has exactly the 48 symmetries of a cube. Show its Laplace eigenvalues repeat no more often than those symmetries force (at most 3 times), except possibly for finitely many eigenvalues.
math: Let $S=\{x^4+y^4+z^4=1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the induced metric (isometry group the hyperoctahedral group of order 48, whose irreducible representations have dimension $\le3$). Prove that all but finitely many eigenvalues of $\Delta_S$ have multiplicity $\le3$.

title: Frozen vortices for Kuramoto on a cube
plain: Identical Kuramoto oscillators sit on the grid of a cube's surface. Besides full synchrony, there is a 'longitude' state with a vortex at the centre of the top face and an antivortex at the centre of the bottom face. Prove that this state is a linearly stable equilibrium for every grid size.
math: Let $Q_n$ be the vertex–edge graph of the $n\times n$ subdivided surface of the cube, and $\dot\theta_i=\sum_{j\sim i}\sin(\theta_j-\theta_i)$. Prove that for every odd $n\ge3$ there is an equilibrium $\theta^*$ with the cube's 4-fold rotational symmetry about the vertical axis and winding number $\pm1$ around the central plaquettes of the top and bottom faces, whose Jacobian (the Laplacian with edge weights $\cos(\theta^*_j-\theta^*_i)$) has kernel exactly $\mathrm{span}(\mathbf 1)$ and is otherwise positive. (More generally: for which $n$ does $Q_n$ have a stable non-synchronous equilibrium?)

title: Two vortices on a cube
plain: Two identical point vortices moving on the surface of a cube form a two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system with no continuous symmetry, so there is no second conserved quantity to make it integrable. Prove their motion is genuinely chaotic.
math:
Let $S$ be the boundary of the unit cube with its flat cone metric (eight cone points $v_i$ of angle $3\pi/2$), area $A=6$. Let $G$ solve $-\Delta_zG(z,w)=\delta_w-1/A$ with $\int_SG(\cdot,w)\,dA=0$, and let $R(z)=\lim_{w	o z} ig[G(z,w)+	frac1{2\pi}\log d(z,w) ig]$ for $z
otin\{v_i\}$. On $M=\{(z_1,z_2):z_1

otin\{v_i\}\}$ with $\omega=dA(z_1)+dA(z_2)$, let $H=G(z_1,z_2)+	frac12(R(z_1)+R(z_2))$. Prove that the Hamiltonian flow has a compact invariant set, inside one energy level, on which its topological entropy is positive.

title: Non-flat free-boundary minimal disks in the superball
plain: In a round ball the only free-boundary minimal disks are flat slices through the centre (Nitsche). The superball x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1 has nine flat ones, cut by its mirror planes. Is there also one that is not flat? A natural candidate has threefold symmetry about the diagonal (1,1,1).
math: For $p>2$ let $B_p=\{|x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p\le1\}$. Decide whether $B_4$ (more generally $B_p$) contains an embedded minimal disk $\Sigma$ with $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial B_p$, meeting $\partial B_p$ orthogonally, that is not contained in a plane. Specifically, show that there is one invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/3$ about the axis $\mathbb R(1,1,1)$ and under $v\mapsto-v$.

title: Rotation-proof lattice-point-poor shapes
plain: Among convex shapes of area A, how few lattice points can a shape be guaranteed to contain under every rotation about the origin? Can any shape do much better than a disc centred at the origin?
math: For $A>0$ let $m(A)=\inf\{\sup_{\theta}\#(\rho_\theta K\cap\mathbb Z^2): K\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ compact convex},\ |K|=A\}$. Decide whether $m(A)\ge A-O_\varepsilon(A^{1/4+\varepsilon})$.

title: Rupert superballs
plain: A cube can pass through a hole drilled in a copy of itself; a round ball cannot. Show that every superball between them, |x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p ≤ 1 with p > 2, can.
math: Let $B_p=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x_1|^p+|x_2|^p+|x_3|^p\le1\}$ and $q=p/(p-1)$. Prove that for every $p\in(2,\infty)$ there are orthogonal projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of $\mathbb R^3$ onto planes and a rigid motion $\rho$ with $\rho(\pi_1(B_p))\subset\operatorname{int}\pi_2(B_p)$. By central symmetry this is equivalent to: there are orthonormal pairs $(a_1,a_2),(b_1,b_2)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ with $\|\cos t\,b_1+\sin t\,b_2\|_q>\|\cos t\,a_1+\sin t\,a_2\|_q$ for all $t$.

title: Prime Markov triples
plain: Markov triples are positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Are there infinitely many in which all three numbers are prime?
math: Decide whether infinitely many solutions $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^3$ of $x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz$ have $x,y,z$ all prime.

title: Burgers with degenerate critical dissipation
plain: Critical half-Laplacian dissipation keeps Burgers smooth. Let that dissipation switch off quadratically at one point of the circle. Do shocks form there?
math: Let $a(x)=1-\cos x$ and consider $u_t+uu_x+\Lambda^{1/2}\big(a\,\Lambda^{1/2}u\big)=0$ on $\mathbb{T}$, $\Lambda=(-\partial_x^2)^{1/2}$. Decide whether every real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ yields a global smooth solution.

title: Minimal-mass blow-up with reflection
plain: Consider the 2D Schrödinger equation in which the self-interaction at each point uses the density at the mirror point -x. Below the ground-state mass, solutions exist forever. Show that the only solutions that blow up with exactly the ground-state mass are the explicit pseudo-conformal ground-state solutions centred at the origin.
math: Let $Q>0$ be the radial solution of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Consider $iu_t+\Delta u+|u(-x,t)|^2u=0$ with $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^2)$ and $\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$. Prove that if $u$ blows up at a finite time $T$, then there are $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\lambda>0$ with $u(t,x)=e^{i\theta}\frac{\lambda}{T-t}\,Q\!\Big(\frac{\lambda x}{T-t}\Big)\exp\!\Big(i\frac{\lambda^2}{T-t}-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}\Big)$.

title: Riesz-transform Schrodinger equation
plain: Couple a 2D Schrodinger wave to the Riesz transform of its own density. Mass is conserved, but there is no energy. Do smooth solutions live forever?
math: Consider $iu_t+\Delta u=u\,R_1(|u|^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^2$, $\widehat{R_1f}(\xi)=-i\frac{\xi_1}{|\xi|}\hat f(\xi)$. Decide whether every $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$ gives a global solution in $C(\mathbb{R},H^1)$.

title: Shifted Fujita equation
plain: In the plane, every positive solution of u_t = Delta u + u^2 blows up (u^2 is exactly Fujita-critical in dimension 2). Does this survive when u^2 is replaced by the product of the values of u one unit to the left and one unit to the right?
math: Let $e=(1,0)$. Prove or disprove: for every $0\le u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^2)$ with $u_0\not\equiv0$, the solution of $u_t=\Delta u+u(x-e,t)\,u(x+e,t)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ blows up in finite time.

title: Unforced blow-up near the forced one
plain: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a force that is smooth through the blow-up time. Can the force be made to vanish identically at the blow-up instant while staying smooth up to and including that instant?
math: Do there exist $T>0$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty))$ with $f(\cdot,T)\equiv0$ such that the 3D Navier–Stokes solution on $\mathbb R^3$ with $u_0=0$ and force $f$ satisfies $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$? (Requiring $f\equiv0$ on $[T-\delta,T]$ for some $\delta>0$ instead would be equivalent to unforced blow-up from smooth data, which is the Millennium problem.)

title: Random Wang tiles
plain: (Corrected.) Draw n Wang tiles whose four edge colours are chosen uniformly at random from c colours, and let c grow with n ≈ λc². How likely is the set to tile the plane? Show the probability has a limit F(λ) and find the critical λ above which tiling is almost certain.
math: Let $T_1,\dots,T_n$ be i.i.d. Wang tiles, each with its four edge colours i.i.d. uniform in $[c]$ and no rotations allowed. Let $n=\lfloor\lambda c^2\rfloor$ and $c\to\infty$. Prove that $F(\lambda)=\lim_{c\to\infty}\Pr(\{T_i\}\text{ tiles }\mathbb Z^2)$ exists for every $\lambda>0$. Determine $\lambda_c=\inf\{\lambda:F(\lambda)=1\}$; a first-moment heuristic suggests $\lambda_c=1$. Also determine $F$ on $(0,\lambda_c)$.

title: Period-doubling torus bundles
plain: Build a once-punctured torus bundle by reading the period-doubling word as a product of the two basic shear matrices. Show its hyperbolic volume per letter settles to a limit as the word grows.
math: Let $W_n\in\{a,b\}^{2^n}$ be the length-$2^n$ prefix of the fixed point of $a\mapsto ab,\ b\mapsto aa$ ($n\ge1$). Let $\phi_n\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ be the product obtained from $W_n$ via $a\mapsto R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $b\mapsto L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and let $M_n$ be the once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy $\phi_n$ (hyperbolic since $W_n$ contains both letters). Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(M_n)/2^n$ exists.

title: Thue–Morse Lorenz knots
plain: Turn the first 2^n letters of the Thue–Morse word into a periodic orbit of the Lorenz flow, and so into a knot K_n. For n >= 4 these knots appear to be hyperbolic. Their volume grows only in proportion to n, the logarithm of the word length, not in proportion to the length itself. Prove that, and find the constant.
math: Let $K_n$ be the Lorenz knot with Lorenz word $t_0t_1\cdots t_{2^n-1}$ (the length-$2^n$ Thue–Morse prefix, $0\mapsto x$, $1\mapsto y$; this word is primitive, since Thue–Morse is overlap-free and $t_{[0,2^n)}=w\bar w$). Prove that $S^3\setminus K_n$ is hyperbolic for all $n\ge4$ and that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(S^3\setminus K_n)/n$ exists and is positive. Determine the limit.

title: Odd plus odd is even
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: The sum of two odd natural numbers is even.
math: For all $a,b\in\mathbb N$, if $a$ and $b$ are odd then $a+b$ is even.

title: n² + n is even
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: For every integer n, the number n² + n is even.
math: For all $n\in\mathbb Z$, $2\mid n^2+n$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 4 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Sum of the first n odd numbers
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Adding up the first n odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … gives n².
math: For all $n$, $\sum_{i<n}(2i+1)=n^2$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 8 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Nicomachus: sum of cubes
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n numbers.
math: For all $n$, $\sum_{i=0}^{n} i^3=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n} i\right)^2$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 16 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Coins of 3 and 5
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Every whole number from 8 upward can be paid exactly with coins worth 3 and 5.
math: For every $n\ge 8$ there are $a,b\in\mathbb N$ with $n=3a+5b$.

title: Party of six (R(3,3) ≤ 6)
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Among any six people, some three all know each other or some three are all strangers.
math: Every simple graph on 6 vertices contains a triangle or an independent set of size 3.

title: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequences
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Any list of rs + 1 distinct real numbers has an increasing run of r + 1 of them or a decreasing run of s + 1 of them (not necessarily consecutive).
math: For $f:\{0,\dots,rs\}\to\mathbb R$ injective there is a set of $r+1$ indices on which $f$ is strictly increasing, or a set of $s+1$ indices on which it is strictly decreasing.

title: Dilworth's theorem
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: In any finite partially ordered set, the largest number of pairwise incomparable elements equals the smallest number of chains needed to cover everything.
math: For every finite poset $P$ there are $k$, an antichain of size $k$, and a partition of $P$ into $k$ chains.
